identification.name: Stainless Steel 17-4 PH (Condition H1025)
identification.common_form_notes: Commonly stocked as round bar in the as-annealed Condition A (e.g. McMaster-Carr, per ASTM A564/AMS 5643) — NOT pre-aged. Machine in the softer annealed state, then age-harden (single furnace cycle, ~4 h at 1025°F/552°C for H1025) afterward for minimal dimensional change. The properties stored here are for the aged H1025 condition; as-purchased/as-machined stock is significantly weaker (~Rockwell C30 vs. H1025's C38) until that heat-treat step is done.
identification.notes: A precipitation-hardening (PH) stainless — selected deliberately for a specific combination of high strength and good corrosion resistance, not a routine/default stainless choice like 303/304/316. H1025 (aged at 1025°F/552°C) was chosen as the representative condition: the most commonly specified general-purpose temper, balancing strength, toughness, and corrosion/stress-corrosion-cracking resistance better than the higher-strength but less tough H900 condition. Strength/hardness/elongation are from AK Steel's Condition H1025-specific datasheet (these vary significantly with aging condition). Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, and CTE (coefficient of thermal expansion) are essentially condition-independent (aging affects strength via precipitate formation, not elastic stiffness) and are cross-validated across three sources: AZoM (E 190–210 GPa, ν 0.27–0.30, shear modulus 77.4 GPa — back-calculating E from G and ν gives ≈198 GPa, consistent) and Wikipedia (E 197–207 GPa, density 7800–7900 kg/m³, both agreeing closely with AK Steel's H1025 density of 7.80 g/cm³). Thermal conductivity (17.9 W/m·K) is AZoM's value explicitly labeled for Condition H900, used here as a reasonable estimate since thermal conductivity doesn't vary much with aging condition — flagged since it isn't H1025-specific. Usable temperature max (300 °C) is Wikipedia's stated corrosion-resistance service limit, not a distinct mechanical-property limit. Shear strength derived via von Mises: UTS (ultimate tensile strength)/√3 = 1276/1.732 ≈ 737 MPa. Magnetic (ferromagnetic) due to its martensitic structure — a notable difference from the austenitic 303/304/316 grades already in this database, which are only weakly (para)magnetic.

typical_usage: High-strength, corrosion-resistant machined parts: shafts, fasteners, valve components, pump parts, and structural fittings in marine/ROV (remotely operated vehicle)/AUV (autonomous underwater vehicle) applications where 303/304/316 don't offer enough strength. Common in aerospace and firearms industries for the same strength/corrosion-resistance combination. Choose a lower-aging-temperature condition (e.g. H900) instead if maximum strength matters more than toughness/corrosion resistance; choose a higher one (H1075/H1150) if the reverse. Costs noticeably more than 303/304/316 (specialty melting practice plus a required aging heat treatment) and needs an extra manufacturing step — only worth it when the part genuinely needs strength an austenitic grade can't reach. Choose 17-7 PH instead if the part must be cold-formed (bent, deep-drawn) before hardening; 17-4 PH's simpler single-step aging is preferable when the part is machined rather than formed to shape.
